contract: 1. Outcomes. Every program launch and every call a reader finds in a scanned file is approved, known or refused. Approved: a row in 'approved' allows it in the form written, and it needs no list entry. Known: a row in 'programs' allows it in the form written, and it needs an exact-line entry in the known list that names that row. Refused: no row allows it, and it needs an exact-line reasoned exception whose reason is true of that line. A line that has a refused call needs a reason even if its other calls are approved or known. A file a reader cannot parse, or a code file of a type no reader reads, fails the check, and no entry clears it.

2. What a row may allow. A row names one program, cmdlet or fully resolved call, and the subcommands, options and argument shapes under which it cannot walk a tree, enter a link while walking, make a link, mount a volume, map a drive, make a share or a virtual disk, or change a permission or an owner. Walking a tree means listing or acting on what lies below the entries of a folder it is given, or matching a wildcard against folder names. Opening, reading, writing, renaming or deleting one named file or empty folder, and listing the entries of one named folder, is not a walk. When in doubt the row is left out and the lines carry reasons.

3. Programs ('programs', and the bash and cmd rows in 'approved'). A program matches its row only when it is named by its bare name or by a literal absolute path; .exe or .com may follow the name. If the row has 'subcommands', the first argument must be one of them, written literally, and the rest is matched against that subcommand's row. Every argument that starts with the row's switch characters ('-' unless 'switch' says otherwise) must be one of its 'options', written exactly (in any case unless the row says 'case': 'sensitive'); 'flag' takes no value, a number takes that many following arguments, and any other kind takes one value that must fit it. Every other argument is an operand and must fit 'operands'; a row without 'operands' takes none. A computed argument counts as a possible option, so it matches only where 'operands' is 'any'. 'literal': n requires the first n arguments to be literal and not to start with '-'. Kinds: 'any' (computed allowed), 'literal' (any literal), 'plain' (a literal with no * ? [ or `), 'name' (an identifier that is not PSDefaultParameterValues, PATH, PATHEXT or PSModulePath), or a list of literal values.

4. PowerShell cmdlets ('approved' 'powershell'). A row given as text allows the cmdlet in every form, so only cmdlets that take no file path and load no code get one. Otherwise a line matches only if every parameter is written by its exact full name (in any case) from 'params' or the common parameters, and its value fits the kind there ('switch' needs no value; 'block' needs a script block literal); arguments without a parameter name bind in order to 'positional' (the 'remaining' one takes the rest); a splat matches nothing; a cmdlet that is not the first element of a pipeline matches only a row with 'pipeline'; a row with 'bound' matches only when one of those parameters is bound on the line. The aliases in 'powershell aliases' match their cmdlet's row, except those in 'powershell platform aliases', which name programs on Linux and macOS and so match no cmdlet row.

5. Calls. A .NET, Python, native or workflow row names the exact resolved call; a method called on a value whose type the reader cannot tell is matched by its name alone ('python methods', 'powershell methods'), so a name that some known type implements unsafely is never on those two lists. Every condition in a row's 'args' must hold: 'in' (the argument is a literal in the list), 'absent' (the argument may be left out), 'types' (the argument's static type), 'one folder' (a literal with no wildcard in any folder part), 'literal not in' (a literal not in the list).

6. Functions. A PowerShell or bash call runs a repo function, and needs nothing, only when an unconditional definition of that name is in effect at the call: a direct statement of its file that comes before the call or before any code of that file runs, a direct statement of the function body that holds the call and comes before it, or a direct statement of a script dot-sourced before the call. A name that Set-Alias or the function: or alias: drive may rename in scope resolves to no function. Every other call is matched as the cmdlet or program of that name. A repo function (PowerShell, Python, C# or bash) that starts a program named by one of its parameters, or gives a parameter to one of the 'runners' (programs that run a program or code from their arguments), is a launcher: every call to it is refused too, and so is every call that passes its own parameters on to a launcher.

7. Refused because the parser cannot resolve them, so only a reasoned exception clears them: dynamic invocation (reflection, a delegate built at run time, getattr, a method group's Invoke, Invoke-Expression, Add-Type, text parsed into code); a shell or interpreter given text; a program, subcommand or parameter name the reader cannot read as a literal; a splat; a definition made conditionally or at run time where no unconditional one is in effect; a dot-source of a script from a folder the reader cannot read (the script it names is still read); and every syntax node kind a reader has no rule for (Python ast node types, C# operation kinds, PowerShell AST types, bash syntax node types, workflow keys; cmd and MSBuild refuse what they cannot read).

foreach-object.does: runs a script block it is given for each object; the block is read in place as code of this file

invoke-command.does: runs a script block it is given in this session; the block is read in place as code of this file

start-job.does: runs a script block it is given in a background PowerShell; the block is read in place as code of this file

set-variable.does: sets a variable named by a literal

join-path.does: joins path text in memory; without -Resolve it reads no folder

split-path.does: splits path text in memory; without -Resolve it reads no folder

resolve-path.does: resolves one path to its full form

get-childitem.does: lists the items of one folder; without -Recurse or -Depth it enters no folder below it

get-acl.does: reads the permissions of one item

get-authenticodesignature.does: reads the signature of one file

get-itempropertyvalue.does: reads one property of one item

set-itemproperty.does: sets one property of one item

new-itemproperty.does: adds one property to one item

remove-itemproperty.does: removes one property of one item

remove-item.does: deletes one file or empty folder; without -Recurse it deletes nothing below a folder

copy-item.does: copies one file, or one folder without its contents; without -Recurse it copies nothing below a folder

new-item.does: makes one file or folder; it interprets no wildcard in -Path

select-string.does: searches text, or the files it is given by path

tee-object.does: passes objects on and writes them to one file or variable

start-transcript.does: records the session to one file

get-command.does: looks up a command by a literal name

powershell.out-null: returns nothing; it only discards what it is given
powershell.out-string: turns objects into text in memory
powershell.write-verbose: writes a message to the verbose stream
powershell.where-object: filters objects in memory; a script block it is given is read in place as code of this file
powershell.select-object: selects objects or their properties in memory
powershell.measure-object: counts or sums objects in memory
powershell.convertto-json: turns objects into JSON text in memory
powershell.convertto-csv: turns objects into CSV text in memory
powershell.convertto-securestring: turns text into a secure string in memory
powershell.add-member: adds a property or method to an object in memory
powershell.new-timespan: makes a time span in memory
powershell.pop-location: returns to a location this script pushed
powershell.wait-process: waits for a process to end
powershell.get-ciminstance: reads WMI or CIM objects; it calls no method on them
powershell.export-scheduledtask: returns a scheduled task as XML text
powershell.new-scheduledtasktrigger: makes a task trigger object in memory
powershell.new-scheduledtasksettingsset: makes a task settings object in memory
powershell.new-scheduledtaskprincipal: makes a task principal object in memory

bash.:: a bash builtin that does nothing
bash.break: a bash builtin that leaves a loop
bash.continue: a bash builtin that continues a loop
bash.cd: a bash builtin that changes the current folder
bash.echo: a bash builtin that prints its words
bash.exit: a bash builtin that ends the script
bash.pwd: a bash builtin that prints the current folder
bash.return: a bash builtin that returns from a function
bash.set: a bash builtin that sets shell options or the positional words
bash.shift: a bash builtin that drops positional words
bash.wait: a bash builtin that waits for child processes

read.does: a bash builtin that reads a line into variables named by literals

ping.does: sends echo requests to a host; scripts use it to wait

sleep.does: waits for a number of seconds

jq.does: reads JSON from its input or the files it names and prints what its filter selects; it runs no program

mktemp.does: makes one temporary file or folder

dirname.does: prints the folder part of a path

basename.does: prints the last part of a path

realpath.does: prints the resolved form of a path

head.does: prints the start of its input or the files it names

tail.does: prints the end of its input or the files it names

date.does: prints the date in a literal format

dotnet.does: prints the installed .NET runtimes, SDKs or version

data.json: data the code reads; nothing runs it
